sentences.say: These days, almost everyone works with an AI assistant.
It helps us write code and find answers faster.
But each of us uses it in our own way, and what one person learns stays with that person.
So working as a team takes more care than before.
If a team wants to work with AI together, there are five things worth sharing.
The first one is the workflow: the way the work moves.
You say what you need, in your own words, to one agent: the orchestrator.
It turns that into clear steps, and hands each step to the agent that knows that area best.
Every one of those agents is built in the same way,
and they all report back in the same form.
Around them, a few fixed rules in code make sure nothing goes off course.
The second thing to share is standards.
When everyone follows the same patterns, the work comes out the same, no matter who asked for it.
The results are structured, so the next agent can pick them up right away,
and they are also easy for people to read: commits, pull requests, docs.
The team even shares the same tools.
Third, knowledge.
Gaia starts out knowing nothing about your work. It learns as you go.
It scans each project to understand how it is built,
it keeps the decisions you have made,
it remembers what was left open,
and it saves every piece of work in a clear, structured way, so it can be found later.
Fourth, being able to see where things stand.
Every idea is written down, so it does not get lost in a chat.
It becomes a plan,
the plan becomes small tasks, and each task comes with its own test.
At the end, a different agent checks the result, one that did not do the work.
And fifth, audit: knowing who answers for what.
When a change really matters, a person is in charge, and has to approve it.
Every step leaves a trail you can follow,
every piece of work gets a grade,
and bad habits are flagged, so they can be fixed.
Those five things are what Gaia brings to a team.
Now, let's see how it does it.
Let's start with the question itself: what is Gaia?
Gaia is a layer that sits between you and your AI agents.
It talks with you and coordinates the work, but it never makes the changes itself.
You only talk to one agent: the orchestrator. There is one per session.
It listens to what you want, in your own words, and decides what has to happen.
Before it starts, it shows you the route, so you can change it on the way.
But the orchestrator never edits a file.
It hands the work to a specialist, the agent that knows that field best.
There are eight today: one for code, one for infrastructure, one for live systems, and more. You can add your own.
Each one starts clean, for one piece of work. When it is done, it sends back a contract: a report in a fixed form.
Starting clean does not mean starting empty.
The moment a specialist starts, Gaia hands it five things.
Its identity: what it is for, and what it may touch.
Its skills: the team's way of doing that kind of work.
The project context: what Gaia knows about the project, and which parts it may read or write.
What Gaia knows about you: your rules and preferences, so it does not ask you again.
And its contract, open from the start: the goal, and the form it has to fill in.
While the work runs, rules in code keep watch.
If a specialist needs to change something that matters, Gaia stops it and shows you the exact command, what it changes, and how to undo it.
Nothing runs until you answer.
And when the specialist reports back, its contract is checked before the orchestrator uses it for the next step.
Then Gaia keeps what should outlive the session.
The decisions you made and why, what was learned, the work still open, and how you like to work.
Ideas become plans, and plans become tasks that another agent checks before they count as done.
So the next session starts where this one ended.
All of this runs through one tool: Gaia's own command line.
Next, let's look closer at what Gaia knows.
What do you know about my work?
Gaia starts with nothing. Everything it knows, it learned while working with you.
It keeps that in four memories, and each one answers a simple question.
The first one asks: what do we know about the project, and about you?
When you open a project, Gaia scans the workspace and its repositories, and writes down what it finds, section by section.
Each specialist is told which of those sections it may read, and which it may write.
It also keeps what is yours: your rules, your preferences, and the decisions you made, with the reason behind them.
The second asks: what are we doing, and what is still open?
Bigger work starts as a brief: a short page that says what you want, and how you will know it is done.
The brief becomes one plan,
and the plan is split into tasks. Each task carries its own checks, called gates.
If the plan has to change, the change is recorded, and the earlier version is kept.
And whatever is paused, blocked or pending carries forward to the next session.
The third asks: what did we do, and what came out of it?
Every turn ends with its contract: how it ended, and the evidence behind it.
Every change you approved is kept, with your answer.
And every check leaves its verdict: pass or fail, and what is still open.
Together, they form an audit trail you can follow later.
The fourth asks: what happened, and when?
This one nobody writes. Gaia's engine records it on its own, as events, turns and sessions.
Put in order, they become a timeline.
Anything unusual is flagged, and a turn that was cut short is marked, so nothing disappears quietly.
And each new session starts with the last twenty-four hours.
These four memories are not separate boxes.
A single task leaves a trace in all four: in the project it touched, in the plan it belongs to, in its contract, and in the record of its turn.
You decide what is worth keeping. The engine records the rest.
But knowing is not enough. What happens when the work needs to change something?
Let's follow one request, from your question to the result.
It starts with you: you ask for something, in your own words.
Next, the orchestrator, the agent you talk to, sends the job to a specialist.
Before it starts, Gaia gives it what it needs: the goal, your rules, and a form to fill in.
Then the specialist does the work.
It reads files, edits code, and runs tests.
All the while, Gaia checks every action with fixed rules.
Safe actions go through, so you are not asked.
Now the specialist wants to push the code.
That changes something other people use.
So Gaia stops it, and the specialist waits.
This is where you come in: the orchestrator asks you.
Gaia writes the question, and checks it word for word.
You see who asks, the exact command, and how to undo it.
Let's say you approve.
Gaia writes down your answer.
It works once, for this command only.
With that, the specialist continues where it stopped.
The command runs, exactly as you approved it.
Gaia checks the specialist's report.
And only then does the orchestrator tell you the result.
Nothing that matters runs without you seeing it.
How do your agents report back?
You have seen it on every page: each turn ends with a report. Gaia calls it a contract.
It is a form, the same for every agent, so the next one can read it without guessing.
The first thing the form says is how the turn ended:
done, needs a check, needs your approval, needs an answer, blocked, or still working.
That one word tells the orchestrator what to do next.
Then comes the evidence.
The files it read, what it searched, the commands it ran,
what it found, and the exact output, word for word.
So every claim comes with its proof.
The form also says how the work was checked,
what is still open, what else it touched, and the exact command, if it needs your approval.
Before anyone relies on it, Gaia's engine checks the form by rule. A missing or unfinished one sends the agent back.
Then the orchestrator reads it, and decides the next step.
And when the work needs proof, a verifier, a different agent, tests it from the evidence alone.
A report can also update what Gaia knows about the project.
That lives in a second contract: one per workspace, organized in sections.
Its identity: the name, the path, the repository, the language.
Its stack: the languages, the frameworks, the build tools.
Its git setup, and ten more sections like these.
Each agent may only write the sections that belong to its field.
And every contract is kept.
Months later, you can still see who did what, how it was checked, and what it was based on.
That is how Gaia works inside.
So, how do you start?
Starting is simple.
In Claude Code, Gaia is one plugin: you add the marketplace, and you install it.
The first time, you reload the plugins, and that's it.
If you prefer npm, or you use OpenCode, you install the package and connect it to your workspace.
And if you ever want to remove it, there is one command for that too.
Then you just ask, in your own words: what is Gaia?
It explains itself, with everything you just saw.
You don't have to study it first. You ask it.
From there, it grows with you.
On the first session, it maps your repositories by itself.
Then you state a problem, and it finds the project and the right specialist.
And for bigger work, it plans, delegates, and asks before it changes anything.
And you keep talking to Claude Code, the way you already do.
And all of it stays yours.
Everything Gaia learns lives in one database, on your machine, and uninstalling never deletes it.
The code is open source, so your agents and your skills are yours too.
It runs in Claude Code and OpenCode, and one install reaches all your projects.
And the questions people ask first have short answers.
Only one project? One or many.
How does it know my repos? One scan maps them.
Is it safe? Reads run, and changes wait for you.
And if I uninstall? What it learned stays in your database.
So, what could Gaia do for you?
Ask it.
